kaikki_vikisozluk.t:
Extended form of الله (allāh). The origin of the ـُمَّ (-umma) is unknown. Most likely, it is a fossilized remnant of a vocative particle—akin to the very common vocative particle يا (yā)—which would have been productive in earlier Arabic. While a vocative suffix of ـُمَّ (-umma) is not attested in any other extant Arabic word, such a suffix did exist in other ancient Semitic languages such as Ugaritic and carried a vocative meaning (both the equivalents of Arabic يا (yā) and ـُمَّ (-umma) existed as ways to form the vocative in Ugaritic).
Other theories include a connection with مَا (mā), or a borrowing from Hebrew אלוהים (elohim), where the final -m is a majestic plural ending. The form is first attested in the Quran (3:26, 5:114, 8:32, 10:10, 39:46). Classical Arabic philologists in the medieval period often also struggled to determine the word’s etymology, with some, including Sibawayh, suggesting it came from a fusion of الله أُمَّـ (allāh ʔumma-), shortened from يَا أَللّٰهُ أُمَّنَا بِخَيْرٍ (yā ʔallāhu ʔummanā biḵayrin, “O God, lead us in goodness”).
s: 1948, A.D. Singer, “The Vocative in Ugaritic”, in Journal of Cuneiform Studies, page 1:
g: O God; vocative form of الله (allāh) used in invocations, oaths, etc.
